A contradiction is when two things are so directly opposite that both cannot be true, valid, or real at the same time.

Think of it this way: if you say "the light is on" and someone else says "the light is off" — about the same light, at the same moment — those two statements are a contradiction. One must be false. There is no middle ground where both can coexist.

That's the core idea: mutual cancellation. Each side wipes out the other.

Not every disagreement is a contradiction. If you say "I prefer mangoes" and your friend says "I prefer bananas," that's a difference of opinion — both can be true at the same time. No contradiction.

A contradiction requires direct opposition — where one side logically destroys the other. If you say "I never eat fruit" and then someone sees you eating a mango, those two things cannot both be true. That's a contradiction.

The test is simple: can both things exist or be true at the same time? If yes — no contradiction. If no — contradiction.

1. Between statements or claims

A witness in court says, "I was home all night." Security footage shows them at a shop at midnight. These two claims are a contradiction — both cannot be true. At least one is false.

If a friend tells you "I never gossip" and you later hear them gossiping, their words and their actions are in contradiction.

2. Between words and behavior

A parent shouts at their child, "Stop yelling in the house!" The action (yelling) directly contradicts the instruction. This is one of the most common and relatable kinds of contradiction in everyday life.

A leader who publicly preaches honesty while privately deceiving people is a contradiction between what they say and what they do.

3. Within a single idea or phrase — a "contradiction in terms"

Sometimes the contradiction is baked right into the words themselves. A phrase like "honest thief" is a contradiction in terms — honesty and stealing are so opposed that the two words cancel each other out. The thing being described cannot logically exist.

Other examples: "free prisoner," "dry water," "exact estimate." The moment you put these words together, one half destroys the other.

4. In logic — a statement that defeats itself

"This circle is a square." A circle is, by definition, not a square. This isn't just wrong — it's a contradiction, because it describes something that cannot possibly exist. No matter what, it is always false. It self-destructs.

This is why in debates and arguments, saying "that's a contradiction" is such a powerful objection. It doesn't just mean "you're wrong." It means: "You're holding two positions that cannot both be right. Your argument has collapsed from within."
A Person Can Be a Contradiction

You'll often hear someone described as "a walking contradiction." This means their personality, beliefs, or behavior contains deeply opposing forces that clash with each other.

A doctor who chain-smokes. A person who speaks passionately about the environment but wastes resources carelessly. A politician who campaigns for poverty relief while living in extreme luxury. These are all people whose lives contain a contradiction — what they are or do directly opposes what they claim to be or believe.

Calling someone "a walking contradiction" isn't necessarily an insult — it's an observation that two opposing truths exist in the same person at the same time, which feels strange or uncomfortable to witness.

These words are easy to mix up, so understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "contradiction" significantly.

Contradiction vs. Inconsistency

An inconsistency is milder — it means something is uneven, irregular, or doesn't fully match up, but not necessarily in direct opposition. A person who keeps their promises most of the time but occasionally breaks them is inconsistent. A person who solemnly promises something and then immediately does the exact opposite is in contradiction. Contradiction is the sharp, severe, direct form. Inconsistency is the softer, more gradual form.

Contradiction vs. Paradox

This is the most important distinction. A paradox also involves two things that seem to oppose each other — but when you look deeper, a hidden truth or deeper meaning emerges. For example: "The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know." On the surface, this sounds like a contradiction (learning = knowing less?), but it makes deep sense when you reflect on it. Knowledge reveals the vastness of what remains unknown.

A contradiction offers no such resolution. It simply cannot be reconciled. Both sides just can't be true — full stop. A paradox invites deeper thinking and rewards it. A contradiction blocks you: there is no way to make both sides work.

Contradiction vs. Irony

Irony is about an outcome being the opposite of what was expected or intended. It's about surprise and reversal. A fire station burning down is ironic. But it's not a contradiction — the fire station existing and it burning down are not logically opposed statements. They can both be true at the same time (and they are). Contradiction is about logical incompatibility; irony is about unexpected reversal.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

• "That's a contradiction." — Your two claims cannot both be true; you've undermined your own position.
  • "A contradiction in terms." — A phrase whose own words cancel each other out. The thing described cannot exist.
  • "A walking contradiction." — A person whose behavior, words, or nature contains deeply opposing forces.
  • "In contradiction with / to something." — Directly opposed to or in conflict with something. "Her testimony was in contradiction to the evidence."
  • "There's a contradiction in your argument." — Two pieces of your reasoning are mutually exclusive; one destroys the other.

Knowing these will help you use the word family naturally:

  • Contradict (verb): to say or do the opposite of something; to conflict directly with it. "The new data contradicts the old theory."
  • Contradictory (adjective): describes two things that are in contradiction with each other. "The two eyewitnesses gave contradictory accounts." Also used to describe a single thing containing opposing elements: "He has a contradictory nature — kind in public, harsh in private."
  • Self-contradictory (adjective): describes something that contradicts itself. "The argument was self-contradictory — it used the conclusion to prove the conclusion."

A contradiction is the collision of two things so fundamentally opposed that both cannot be true or real at the same time. It can live between two statements, between words and actions, inside a single phrase, or within a person's character. What makes it distinct from related concepts is that it offers no resolution — it is a hard, unbridgeable conflict. One side must give way.
